To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the true value of corruption is higher than the value measured by any index of corruption; 2) the perception-based indices are the most biased; 3) the experience-based indices are less biased; 4) the government-recorded indices are the least biased.

(1) corruption is not a unitary concept but rather a complex phenomenon that is multidimensional, and (2) the most frequently used indices of perceived corruption, such as Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index (CPI) and the Worldwide Governance Indicators (WGI) are not consistent estimators of corruption, but rather biased estimates of the true value of corruption.

(1) the true level of corruption is lower than the perception-based indices, but higher than the experience-based indices; (2) the true level is higher than the government-recorded indices; (3) the government-recorded and perception-based indices are biased downward; (4) the experience-based indices are biased upward; and (5) the true level has a negative effect on economic growth.
